summary: Explains in more depth how to use IPsec to protect signaling between mobile nodes and home agents in Mobile IPv6. It illustrates packet formats, configuration and processing order. It was updated by RFC 4877.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3776 explains how a roaming IPv6 device and its home agent protect location updates and related messages with IPsec. It specifies packet layouts and the order in which each side processes them.

questions: how is mobile ipv6 protected by ipsec
what is a home agent in mobile ipv6
why use esp for binding updates
what is the alternate care-of address option
subtitle: Required packet formats and processing rules for protecting Mobile IPv6 signaling with IPsec.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 needs to protect location updates between a mobile node and its home agent, but the base specification gives only the main requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies ESP packet formats, policy rules, optional IKE key management, example configurations and the required order for processing packets.
tldr.outcome: Implementations must support the required formats and rules. RFC 3776 was later updated by RFC 4877.

facts.label: Binding Update protection
facts.value: ESP MUST be supported and used

today: RFC 3776 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2004 and was updated by RFC 4877. It builds on Mobile IPv6 as defined in RFC 3775.

sections.title: Why Mobile IPv6 Uses IPsec
sections.content:
A mobile node keeps a home address and receives a care-of address when it connects to a foreign link. It tells its home agent about the current location with a Binding Update, and the home agent replies with a Binding Acknowledgement.

Without protection, attackers could alter or impersonate these messages, intercept traffic, or cause denial of service. The Mobile IPv6 base specification uses IPsec ESP to protect signaling between the mobile node and home agent. RFC 3776 explains packet formats and implementation procedures in more detail.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile device tells its home agent where it can currently be reached. IPsec protects those updates so another device cannot easily change or fake them.

sections.title: Required Protected Packet Formats
sections.content:
A Binding Update sent while the mobile node is away from home uses an IPv6 header with the care-of address, a Destination Options header with the Home Address option, ESP in transport mode, and the Mobility header. The Binding Update also carries an Alternate Care-of Address option so ESP protects the care-of address.

A Binding Acknowledgement uses a type 2 Routing header, ESP in transport mode and the Mobility header. Return-routability messages and optional payload packets use ESP tunnel mode. Prefix discovery uses ESP transport mode around ICMPv6 messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message type has a required order of IPv6, mobility and ESP headers. Both the mobile node and home agent must support these packet layouts.

sections.title: Required Support and Policy Rules
sections.content:
Mobile nodes and home agents MUST support manually configured IPsec security associations. IKEv1 key management MAY be supported. ESP for Binding Updates and Acknowledgements MUST be supported and used; ESP for Home Test and prefix-discovery messages MUST be supported and SHOULD be used.

When matching IPsec policy, a Home Address option counts as the packet's source address and a type 2 Routing header counts as its destination address. Binding Updates and prefix discovery use ESP transport mode with authentication. Return-routability packets use tunnel mode with both encryption and authentication.

When an accepted Binding Update changes the care-of address, the home agent updates the destination used for later tunnel packets. It must base that change only on a Binding Update protected by IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC requires protection for location updates and acknowledgements. It also tells the home agent which address to trust when policy checks run and when the mobile node moves.

sections.title: Dynamic Keys with IKE
sections.content:
If anti-replay protection is required, the RFC says dynamic keying MUST be used. Mobile IPv6 sequence numbers help preserve message order, but the sequence number is 16 bits and can wrap; a home-agent restart can also erase its sequence state.

IKE exchanges use the mobile node's care-of address, while the IPsec associations use its home address. The home agent must check that the IKE identity is authorized to establish associations for that home address, so one mobile node cannot send updates for another.
sections.plainLanguage: Dynamic keys help reject old messages that an attacker might replay. The home agent also checks that the identity asking for a key is allowed to use the related home address.

sections.title: Configuration and Packet Processing
sections.content:
The RFC gives example Security Policy Database and Security Association Database entries for manually configured keys and IKE. The examples show which addresses, protocols, directions and ESP modes select each association.

It also traces packet processing. For an outgoing Binding Update, Mobile IPv6 builds the packet, IPsec protects it, and the addresses are then adjusted so the care-of address appears in the outer IPv6 header. The home agent processes the address option before ESP and then passes the verified update to Mobile IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show which policy entry applies to each message. Processing the headers in the required order lets IPsec check the addresses and protect the correct content.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says implementations may support additional packet formats, but a peer may silently discard a format that it does not recognize. Tunnel mode avoids the 24 bytes of overhead that a Home Address option or Routing header would add for the tunneled packets described.

The RFC notes that DES, mandated by the IPsec standards of its time, is not considered secure, especially when manually configured keys remain in use for a long time. Its security section otherwise points to the Mobile IPv6 base specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra packet formats may not work with every peer. The RFC also warns that the DES encryption algorithm required by the older IPsec standards is not secure.
